item.title: Sea ice variability and links to East Siberian permafrost carbon remobilization during the last glacial-interglacial transition
item.dc:creator: Albin Eriksson, Junjie Wu, Matt O'Regan, Örjan Gustafsson
item.description:
Climate of the Past — matched: polar, Arctic, sea ice, abrupt change, deglaciation, interglacial, permafrost, climate change
Sea ice is an important regulator of the Arctic climate systems. Records of sea ice past instrumental records are necessary to understand how sea ice is altered during past periods of abrupt climate change, and what consequences such changes have on the polar climates. Here, we reconstructed the sea ice cover of the East Siberian Arctic and found that the sea ice extent likely was linked to protecting/eroding permafrost coastlines during the last deglaciation.

item.title: Intra-annual grounding-line migration and retreat: insights from high-resolution satellite and in situ observations over Milne Glacier in the Canadian High Arctic
item.dc:creator: Yulia K. Antropova, Derek Mueller, Sergey V. Samsonov, Alexander S. Komarov, Jérémie Bonneau
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: grounding line, subglacial, ice flow, glacier, Arctic
Arctic glaciers that flow into the ocean are changing rapidly due to climate warming. The grounding line, where these glaciers transition from land to ocean, is critical to their stability. We examined Milne Glacier in the Canadian High Arctic using satellite, field, and modelled data. Our study shows how changes in ice flow and ice bending near the grounding line affect satellite-based mapping of this area and documents a newly discovered grounding-line retreat associated with subglacial ridges.

item.title: Extreme glacier melt on the Central Tibetan Plateau during the summer of 2022: detection and mechanisms
item.dc:creator: Fei Zhu, Meilin Zhu, Lu An
item.description:
Hydrology and earth system sciences — matched: glacier, albedo, mass loss, heat wave
Extreme glacier melt events accelerate mass loss, increase glacier instability, and temporarily increase downstream runoff, potentially alleviating drought conditions. Yet the glacier energy–mass balance in the Geladandong region – a headwater region of the Yangtze River (China's longest river) and one of the source regions feeding Siling Co (Tibet's largest lake) – and its connection to the unprecedented 2022 summer melt remain insufficiently quantified. To address this gap, we integrated in-situ mass balance observations and glacio-meteorological data from a 5700 m monitoring site with an energy-mass balance model and applied a novel dual-threshold framework (based on mean and standard deviation) to identify extreme mass loss/melt events in short-term glacier mass balance records. Our novel methodology identified 2021/22 as a period of extreme mass loss and melt intensity, with melt during the 2022 summer heatwave reaching unprecedented extremes. These heatwaves caused an increase in melt amount of 317.8 mm w.e., amounting to 1.66 and 1.69 times the values recorded for the same period in 2019/20 and 2020/21, respectively. This extreme melt was driven by energy balance anomalies over the glacier surface. In terms of net contributions to the +28.2 W m −2 melt energy anomaly during the three identified heatwave windows, enhanced sensible heat flux was the largest term (+17.0 W m −2 ; 60.3 %), followed by increased net longwave radiation (+14.0 W m −2 ; 49.7 %) and increased net shortwave radiation (+5.1 W m −2 ; 18.1 %) associated with reduced albedo, with negative contributions from latent heat flux and subsurface heat flux. Such anomalies were driven by large-scale atmospheric circulation patterns, specifically the eastward extension and northward displacement of the South Asian High (SAH), together with near-neutral mid-latitude westerlies. This study advances the understanding of glacier mass balance responses to extreme weather and climate events on the central Tibetan Plateau.

item.title: DDA-BNN v1.0: a morphology-aware surrogate model for the optical properties of black carbon-containing particles
item.dc:creator: Payton Beeler, Sam Donald, Laura Fierce
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: surrogate model
We developed a surrogate model to predict how black carbon particles absorb and scatter light based on their size, shape, and mixing with other aerosol species. The model was trained on detailed physics simulations and also estimates uncertainty caused by limited training data and unresolved internal structures. It outperformed common simplified particle assumptions, especially for scattering, and can help target new simulations to improve predictions of black carbon's radiative effects.

item.title: aiLand v1: physics-based land surface emulator with observational fine-tuning
item.dc:creator: Nina Raoult, Ewan Pinnington, Mario Santa Cruz, Florian Pinault, Baudouin Raoult, Natalie Zelenka, … (+7)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: emulator
The land surface shapes our weather and climate by controlling how heat and water move between the ground and the air, so the models representing it matter enormously. But they are costly to run and carry built-in errors. We built a faster artificial-intelligence version of one, then used real measurements from sites worldwide to correct some of these errors. The result stays reliable over years and better captures these heat and water exchanges; a quicker, more accurate tool for forecasting.

item.title: Importance of glacier shrinkage for sustaining runoff in Panj River of Pamir, Central Asia
item.dc:creator: Yun Bai, Min Xu, Shichang Kang, Guanghui WEI, Safarov Mustafo, Xingdong Li
item.description:
Journal of Hydrology Regional Studies — matched: glacier, meltwater, global warming
Study region The study area is the Panj River basin, situated in the upper reaches of the Amu Darya basin. Study focus Glacier and snowmelt runoff are vital for sustaining streamflow in the Panj River Basin, a key cryospheric water source region in Central Asia. However, the impacts of glacier retreat, snow changes, and precipitation variability on long-term runoff remain unclear under global warming. This study applied the Hydrologiska Byråns Vattenbalansavdelning (HBV) model to quantify runoff components, including rainfall, snowmelt, and glacier runoff, and integrated the Budyko framework, scenario simulations, and glacier retreat experiments to assess runoff drivers and the hydrological response to glacier loss. New hydrological insights The results showed that total runoff, rainfall runoff, and snowmelt runoff exhibited significant decreasing trends during 1982–2020, whereas glacier runoff increased, reflecting a temporary compensation effect from enhanced glacier melt under climate warming. Meltwater runoff accounted for 67.9% of total runoff and played an important role in regulating streamflow, particularly during dry years. Attribution analysis revealed that runoff changes were mainly controlled by climatic factors (122.5%), with precipitation being the dominant driver, while human activities (−22.5%) partially offset the decline in runoff. Glacier retreat scenarios indicated that continued glacier loss would reduce summer meltwater supply and may alter the seasonal distribution of runoff, with potential implications for the stability of downstream water supply. The impacts of glacier change on mountain runoff processes and regional water resources provide a basis for understanding potential changes in downstream water availability in Central Asia.

item.title: Development and improvement of a nonhydrostatic spectral model using non-constant coefficient semi-implicit and vertically conservative semi-Lagrangian schemes
item.dc:creator: Hiromasa Yoshimura
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
We have developed a two-dimensional x–z nonhydrostatic spectral model that achieves high computational efficiency by allowing long timesteps. The model incorporates several improvements that enhance numerical stability and accuracy. The model was tested with various cases, and good results were obtained. The model ran stably even in the case of an extremely steep mountain with an average slope of 63.4°. These improvements will be applied to a global atmospheric model in future work.
